criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural community water supply service access and coverage expansion under Tanzania's Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Program (RWSSP).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it analyzes decentralized water governance, intergovernmental fiscal transfer rules, and local planning processes. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing community eligibility and access to water supply infrastructure: intergovernmental grant eligibility conditions and allocation formulae, project eligibility screening rules requiring communities to open a bank account in the district town and deposit an upfront cash capital contribution (cost-recovery/commitment fee rule evaluated by total cash rather than per capita), administrative burdens of stipulated application forms and lack of procedural information at village level, and administrative/political discretion by district officials and ward councillors in selecting beneficiary communities.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical multi-level mixed-methods case study combining fieldwork in four rural districts (July 2008 to August 2009), interviews and group discussions with ministry, district, ward, and village officials and villagers, review of village plans, correlation analysis of national district water budget allocations, and comparison of 40 Phase 1 RWSSP project allocations against ward-level water point mapping coverage data.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports access and exclusion outcomes at district, ward, and village levels, specifically whether unserved and low-coverage rural wards and communities receive or are excluded from RWSSP water supply infrastructure projects and development funds relative to baseline functional water point coverage.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (132 rural districts nationally; 4 rural districts, 40 village water projects, and sampled wards/villages), exposure (grant formulae, upfront cash-deposit and bank-account eligibility preconditions, application procedures, and LGA/councillor selection discretion), outcome (district budget allocation vs unserved share and ward/village inclusion or exclusion in RWSSP Phase 1 water projects), and study design (multi-level mixed-methods empirical case study) are all clearly identifiable.

study_design: Multi-level mixed-methods empirical case study (qualitative interviews, group discussions, document review, water point mapping spatial/coverage comparison, and quantitative budget correlation analysis)
population_and_sample: Rural districts, wards, and villages in Tanzania: national budget allocation across 132 districts; fieldwork in 4 rural districts (Iramba, Nzega, Kigoma Rural, Same; 40 Phase 1 RWSSP village projects analyzed, with in-depth interviews/group discussions in 4 wards in Same and Nzega plus 50% of Same wards)
exposure: Decentralized RWSSP resource and project allocation rules: intergovernmental grant eligibility and allocation formulae, community eligibility screening preconditions (opening a bank account and depositing an upfront cash commitment contribution evaluated by total cash amount), formal application procedures/administrative burdens, and district council/political discretion
outcome: Inclusion or exclusion of unserved/underserved wards and villages in RWSSP Phase 1 rural water supply projects (share of allocated water projects reaching wards in the bottom half of improved water point coverage) and alignment of district water development budgets with unserved population shares
rationale: This empirical mixed-methods study examines how administrative, fiscal, and eligibility rules under Tanzania's decentralized Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Program (RWSSP) govern which rural communities gain access to water supply projects. Beyond macro-decentralization, it directly analyzes rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope — including upfront capital cost-sharing preconditions (opening a bank account and depositing cash evaluated as total cash rather than per capita), application burdens and information gaps, grant allocation formulae, and local administrative/political discretion — and links them empirically to exclusion of low-coverage, smaller, and remote wards/villages from Phase 1 water supply projects. All inclusion criteria (c1-c6) are met.
